issues.legal_issue: A person whose property is proposed to be compulsorily acquired must receive an effective opportunity to be heard on objections before the acquisition declaration is made.
material_facts: The owners submitted written objections to the proposed acquisition.
The acquisition officer adjourned the hearing once but refused a further adjournment requested because the owners’ representative and advocate could not attend.
The officer proceeded without hearing the objectors, and the Government made an acquisition declaration.
issues.conclusion: The failure to provide the hearing required by Section 5A(2) invalidated the acquisition declaration.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5A(1) and 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 give an interested person a substantive right to object and to be heard; the hearing is not an empty formality. Section 6 requires the Government to consider the Collector’s report before making a declaration. Because compulsory-acquisition legislation is ex-proprietary, its requirements are strictly construed. The Court relied on Munshi Singh v. Union of India, Om Prakash v. State of Uttar Pradesh, State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh, Union of India v. Mukesh Hans, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, Dev Saran v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Radhy Shyam v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_proceeding: The State undertook proceedings to acquire privately held property compulsorily.
predicates.affected_person_submitted_objections: A person affected by the proposed acquisition submitted objections to it.
predicates.effective_hearing_denied: The acquisition authority proceeded without giving the objector an effective opportunity to be heard.

issues.definition: When compulsory-acquisition proceedings concern a person who objected and that person was denied an effective hearing, the acquisition declaration is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The acquisition officer’s report on objections must reflect an objective application of mind and make recommendations rather than merely reproduce opposing submissions and reject objections conclusorily.
material_facts: The acquisition officer recorded the owners’ objections and the acquiring body’s response to them.
The officer’s report largely repeated the acquiring body’s allegations and rejected the objections with a general reference to the public interest.
The report contained no meaningful assessment of the objections or recommendations showing that they had been considered.
issues.conclusion: The report did not demonstrate application of mind, and the acquisition declaration could not stand on the basis of that report.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 5A(2) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Collector must report recommendations on the objections and the Government must apply its mind to that report before making a declaration. The report need not be lengthy, but it must reflect objective consideration of relevant factors. The Court relied on Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai and the principles affirmed in Dev Saran v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Radhy Shyam v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_proceeding: The State undertook proceedings to acquire privately held property compulsorily.
predicates.objector_submitted_objections: A person affected by the proposed acquisition submitted objections to it.
predicates.report_lacks_reasoned_assessment: The acquisition officer’s report merely recited submissions or gave a conclusory rejection without showing consideration of the objections.

issues.definition: In compulsory-acquisition proceedings, if an objector’s objections are addressed only by a report lacking reasoned assessment, the acquisition declaration is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition declaration set aside after the time for making a declaration on the original acquisition notification has passed cannot be replaced by a fresh declaration relying on that notification.
material_facts: The Government issued an initial acquisition notification and later made a declaration under it.
The Court set aside the declaration for failure to comply with the hearing requirement.
By the time the Court considered the matter, the State could not rely on the original notification to make a fresh declaration.
issues.conclusion: The State could not rely on the original notification to issue a fresh acquisition declaration, although it remained free to initiate fresh acquisition proceedings in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Constitution Bench ruling in Padma Sundara Rao (Dead) v. State of Tamil Nadu concerning the time limit for making a declaration following an acquisition notification under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_proceeding: The State undertook proceedings to acquire privately held property compulsorily.
predicates.acquisition_declaration_set_aside: A court set aside the declaration made in the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.declaration_period_for_original_notice_e: The time allowed for making a declaration based on the original acquisition notice had passed.

issues.definition: If a court sets aside an acquisition declaration after the time for declaring under the original notice has passed, that notice cannot support a fresh declaration.
